reviewerByRule: Graeham C. Gillin (two-state post that states South Carolina law; never Eric Roden)

Aiken, Wooten) were read. Georgia Rules of Professional Conduct 1.16, 1.5, 1.4 and 1.15(I) and Formal Advisory Opinion 87-5 were read on gabar.org (handbook pages render through Firecrawl; the site's rules index is https://www.gabar.org/general-counsel/georgia-rules-of-professional-conduct and per-rule URLs are https://www.gabar.org/handbook/rule48 etc.). South Carolina Rules 1.16, 1.5, 1.15, 1.4 (Rule 407 SCACR) and SCRCP Rule 11 were read on sccourts.org, which now serves them at /resources/judicial-community/court-rules/ (the old displayRule.cfm URLs 301 there). USCR 4.3 was read from the Council of Superior Court Judges' 2025-03-06 PDF on assets.georgiacourts.gov. Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete (S.C. Ct. App. 1984) and Matter of Tillman (S.C. 1995) were read on Justia; Matter of White (S.C. 1997) on sccourts.org. S.C. Code §§ 37-5-108 and 42-15-90 were read on scstatehouse.gov. Statutes of limitations and comparative-fault rules are reused from facts-1756 / facts-1653 (verified 2026-09-24) and match the writer-profile jurisdiction table. The post's Cornell link (law.cornell.edu/ethics/ga/code/GA_CODE.HTM) no longer exists: it 302s to the generic Wex 'legal ethics' page. rodenlaw.com returns 403 to a bare curl UA but 200 to a browser UA; /contact/, the blog URL and the practice-area links resolve. The live homepage and profile give six offices, not five. No SC appellate opinion squarely awarding quantum meruit to a discharged contingent-fee lawyer was found on Justia or sccourts.org; the SC quantum-meruit statements below rest on Eleazer's reasonable-value rule, Rule 1.16 comment [4] ('subject to liability for payment for the lawyer's services'), Rule 1.5(a), and SC Bar Ethics Advisory Opinion 02-08, and are hedged accordingly.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes, you can fire your personal injury lawyer and hire a new one at almost any stage of your case in both Georgia and South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia Rule of Professional Conduct 1.16(a)(3) ('the lawyer is discharged'); South Carolina Rule 1.16(a)(3) and comment [4], Rule 407 SCACR ('A client has a right to discharge a lawyer at any time, with or without cause, subject to liability for payment for the lawyer's services'); Matter of Tillman, 319 S.C. 461, 462 S.E.2d 283 (1995) ('Rule 1.16(a)(3) explicitly gives the client the right to discharge the attorney at any time, with or without cause')
verifiedClaims.note: Both rules verified verbatim. Georgia's rule text on gabar.org: https://www.gabar.org/handbook/rule48. Tillman: https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/1995/24323-2.html

verifiedClaims.claim: Your right to choose your own attorney is fundamental — no court will force you to keep working with a lawyer you have lost confidence in.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The client's right to discharge is unconditional, but the lawyer's exit from a pending case is not: both states' Rule 1.16(c) says that 'When ordered to do so by a tribunal, a lawyer shall continue representation notwithstanding good cause for terminating the representation,' and Georgia's Uniform Superior Court Rule 4.3(1) lets the judge deny a withdrawal that 'would delay the trial or otherwise interrupt the orderly operation of the court or be manifestly unfair to the client.' Reword to 'no lawyer can refuse to be fired, though a court can control the timing of a withdrawal once a case is in litigation.'
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(c); South Carolina RPC 1.16(c), Rule 407 SCACR; Uniform Superior Court Rule 4.3(1) (Council of Superior Court Judges, rules current to 2025-03-06)
verifiedClaims.note: 'No court will force you' overstates; the court can keep the old lawyer in until a substitution is orderly.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under the Georgia Rules of Professional Conduct and South Carolina's equivalent rules, your current attorney must release your file when you terminate the relationship.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Substance is right (Rule 1.16(d) in both states: 'surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled'), but the link is dead — law.cornell.edu/ethics/ga/code/GA_CODE.HTM now 302-redirects to the generic Wex 'legal ethics' page and the #Rule_1.16 anchor no longer exists. Replace the href with the State Bar of Georgia's rule page, https://www.gabar.org/handbook/rule48.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(d) on gabar.org; South Carolina RPC 1.16(d), Rule 407 SCACR
verifiedClaims.note: curl -L on the Cornell URL: 200 at https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/legal_ethics, i.e. a redirect to an unrelated page. The South Carolina rule can be linked at https://www.sccourts.org/resources/judicial-community/court-rules/appellate/rule-407/rule-116/.

verifiedClaims.claim: Both Georgia and South Carolina treat the attorney-client relationship as one that the client can end at any time, for any reason. You do not need to prove your lawyer did something wrong. You do not need the court's permission. You simply notify your current lawyer that you are terminating the relationship and want your file transferred.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Correct as to the client's decision (SC Rule 1.16 cmt [4]: 'with or without cause'). 'You do not need the court's permission' needs one qualifier: once a lawsuit is pending, the change of counsel itself must go through the court — in Georgia superior court the departing lawyer 'shall submit a written request to an appropriate judge of the court for an order permitting such withdrawal' (USCR 4.3(1)), and in South Carolina 'An attorney may be changed by consent, or upon cause shown, and upon such terms as shall be just, upon application, by order of the Court, and not otherwise' (SCRCP 11(b)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: South Carolina RPC 1.16 comment [4]; USCR 4.3(1); Rule 11(b), SCRCP
verifiedClaims.note: Add 'before a lawsuit is filed' after 'You do not need the court's permission', and let the litigation paragraph that follows carry the court-order step.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia Rule of Professional Conduct 1.16(a) requires an attorney to withdraw when the client fires them. South Carolina Rule of Professional Conduct 1.16 contains nearly identical language.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(a)(3); South Carolina RPC 1.16(a)(3), Rule 407 SCACR (both: 'shall withdraw from the representation of a client if ... the lawyer is discharged')
verifiedClaims.note: The two paragraphs are word-for-word the same.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your lawyer cannot refuse to let you go, and they cannot hold your file hostage to pressure you into staying.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Matter of Tillman, 319 S.C. 461 (1995) (public reprimand for continuing to represent a client who had discharged him and improperly asserting a retaining lien on her file); State Bar of Georgia Formal Advisory Opinion 87-5 ('an attorney may not to the prejudice of a client withhold the client's papers or properties upon withdrawal as security for unpaid fees')
verifiedClaims.note: Both states do recognize a retaining lien (O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14(a); In re Anonymous Member of the S.C. Bar, 287 S.C. 250 (1985)), but neither allows it to be used to the client's prejudice. The sentence is accurate as written.

verifiedClaims.claim: One qualification: if your case is in active litigation and a court date is approaching, the court may require your current attorney to file a motion to withdraw. But this is a procedural step, not a barrier. Courts routinely grant withdrawal motions when the client has already retained new counsel.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The court order is required whenever a case is pending, not only when a court date is approaching: USCR 4.3(1) applies to 'any matter pending in any superior court' and SCRCP 11(b) permits a change of attorney 'by order of the Court, and not otherwise.' Under USCR 4.3(1) the request 'will be granted unless in the judge's discretion to do so would delay the trial or otherwise interrupt the orderly operation of the court or be manifestly unfair to the client'; where the withdrawal is with the client's consent the 10-day objection notice is not required. 'Courts routinely grant' is not sourced; use the rule's own standard.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: USCR 4.3(1)-(2); Rule 11(b), SCRCP
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Once a lawsuit has been filed, the change has to go through the court. In Georgia superior court the departing attorney files a written request for an order permitting withdrawal (Uniform Superior Court Rule 4.3), which the judge grants unless it would delay the trial, disrupt the court's calendar or be manifestly unfair to you; in South Carolina an attorney may be changed by consent or on cause shown, by court order (Rule 11(b), SCRCP). When you have already hired new counsel and consent to the change, this is a procedural step, not a barrier.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Your lawyer should return phone calls and emails within a reasonable time frame — typically 24 to 48 hours.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No rule in either state sets an hours figure. Rule 1.4(a) in both states requires the lawyer to 'keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter' and 'promptly comply with reasonable requests for information.' Drop 'typically 24 to 48 hours' and cite the rule.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.4(a)(3)-(4); South Carolina RPC 1.4(a)(3)-(4), Rule 407 SCACR
verifiedClaims.note: The '24 to 48 hours' figure is traceable to no primary source and reads as a rule. SC rule text: https://www.sccourts.org/resources/judicial-community/court-rules/appellate/rule-407/rule-14/

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia has a two-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. South Carolina allows three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 ('actions for injuries to the person shall be brought within two years after the right of action accrues'); S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1756 / facts-1653 (verified 2026-09-24); matches the writer-profile jurisdiction table. SC: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t15c003.php

verifiedClaims.claim: Both the State Bar of Georgia and the South Carolina Bar maintain public records of disciplinary actions against licensed attorneys.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: yes — discipline runs through the State Bar of Georgia's disciplinary process under Bar Rules 4-101 and 4-102 and is imposed by the Supreme Court of Georgia. South Carolina: lawyer discipline is administered by the Supreme Court of South Carolina through the Commission on Lawyer Conduct and the Office of Disciplinary Counsel, not by the South Carolina Bar (the Bar's own ethics opinions state 'LAWYER DISCIPLINE IS ADMINISTERED SOLELY BY THE SOUTH CAROLINA SUPREME COURT THROUGH ITS COMMISSION ON LAWYER CONDUCT'); public disciplinary opinions are published on sccourts.org. Change 'the South Carolina Bar' to 'the Supreme Court of South Carolina's Office of Disciplinary Counsel'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State Bar of Georgia, Rules 4-101 and 4-102 (Enforcement of the Georgia Rules of Professional Conduct; levels of discipline); South Carolina Judicial Branch, Lawyer & Judicial Discipline; SC Bar EAO 02-08 preamble
verifiedClaims.note: The comparison table already names 'SC Office of Disciplinary Counsel' for South Carolina; make the body consistent with it.

verifiedClaims.claim: Most personal injury attorneys offer free consultations.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Many personal injury attorneys, including Roden Law, offer free consultations.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md trust signals (free case review); no survey supports 'most'
verifiedClaims.note: Frequency claim with no primary source; 'many' is defensible, 'most' is not.

verifiedClaims.claim: Check the termination clause in your contingency fee agreement. Most agreements state that if the client terminates the relationship, the attorney is entitled to compensation for work performed — either on a quantum meruit (reasonable value) basis or through an attorney's lien on the eventual recovery.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Advice is sound; 'Most agreements' is unsourced. The legally important point is what happens when the agreement is silent: in Georgia a discharged contingent-fee lawyer cannot collect under the contract because the contingency never happened, but 'the attorney still has [a] remedy in quantum meruit' (Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 263 Ga. App. 860 (2003)); in South Carolina a lien for the fee on the recovery exists only if the agreement creates one (Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., 281 S.C. 344 (Ct. App. 1984)), which is why reading the termination clause matters more there. Both states require the contingent-fee agreement itself to be in writing (Georgia RPC 1.5(c)(1); SC RPC 1.5(c) 'in a writing signed by the client').
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 263 Ga. App. 860, 589 S.E.2d 626 (2003); Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., 281 S.C. 344, 315 S.E.2d 174 (Ct. App. 1984); Georgia RPC 1.5(c); South Carolina RPC 1.5(c)
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'Most agreements state' to 'Many agreements state', and add one sentence: 'Your agreement must be in writing in both states (Rule 1.5(c)), so the terms should be easy to check.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Your case file belongs to you — medical records, police reports, insurance correspondence, expert reports, deposition transcripts, and all other documents. Both Georgia and South Carolina require attorneys to promptly return client files upon termination under Rule 1.16(d).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Rule 1.16(d) in both states requires 'surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled'; the word 'promptly' is not in either rule. Georgia FAO 87-5 defines what the client is entitled to: original documents and 'any work product intended for use in the case' (in a contingency matter), while the lawyer may keep copies at the lawyer's own expense and may keep internal records such as time records. South Carolina's Rule 1.16(d) adds that the lawyer 'may retain papers relating to the client to the extent permitted by other law' and 'may retain a reasonable nonrefundable retainer.'
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(d); State Bar of Georgia Formal Advisory Opinion 87-5; South Carolina RPC 1.16(d), Rule 407 SCACR
verifiedClaims.note: Reword: 'Both Georgia and South Carolina require an attorney, on termination, to surrender the papers and property the client is entitled to (Rule 1.16(d)). The lawyer may keep a copy of the file at their own expense.' Same fix in the comparison table's 'File return requirement' row.

verifiedClaims.claim: If a lawsuit has been filed, your old attorney must file a motion to withdraw and your new attorney must file a notice of appearance. Courts handle this by consent order when the client has already retained new counsel.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia superior court: the departing attorney submits a written request for an order permitting withdrawal; the request must state that the client received written notice and 10 days passed without objection, 'or that withdrawal is with the client's consent' (USCR 4.3(1)); a notification certificate is filed with the court. South Carolina: 'An attorney may be changed by consent, or upon cause shown ... by order of the Court, and not otherwise. Written notice of change of attorney must be served as provided by Rule 5' (SCRCP 11(b)). 'Courts handle this by consent order' is fair for the consent case; say 'the court can enter the order on consent'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: USCR 4.3(1)-(2); Rule 11(b), SCRCP
verifiedClaims.note: Add the two rule citations so this step is anchored: '(Uniform Superior Court Rule 4.3 in Georgia; Rule 11(b), SCRCP in South Carolina)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: If you signed a contingency fee agreement, your first lawyer will almost certainly claim they are owed something for the work already performed. This does not mean you pay two full contingency fees.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 'Almost certainly' is unsourced; 'may well claim' is enough. The second sentence is right: the discharged lawyer's recovery is the reasonable value of the services, not the contract percentage (Ellerin; Yetman), and any division of a fee between lawyers in different firms requires the client's written agreement and a total fee that is reasonable (Georgia RPC 1.5(e); SC RPC 1.5(e)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 263 Ga. App. 860 (2003); Greer, Klosik & Daugherty v. Yetman, 269 Ga. 271 (1998) (as quoted in Ellerin); Georgia RPC 1.5(e); South Carolina RPC 1.5(e)
verifiedClaims.note: Soften 'will almost certainly claim' to 'may claim'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Here is how it typically works: your first attorney files a lien for the reasonable value of their services. When the case resolves, your new attorney pays the first attorney's lien from the fee portion of the settlement. The total amount paid in attorney fees should not exceed the contingency percentage you originally agreed to. If the two attorneys cannot agree on how to split the fee, the dispute goes to arbitration or court — but that fight is between the two lawyers, not the client.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: the lien attaches to the action and any judgment or recovery (O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14(b)) and the discharged lawyer's fee is measured in quantum meruit, 'value ... defined in terms of value to the recipient' (Ellerin). 'Should not exceed the contingency percentage' is a negotiating norm, not a rule of either state — both states' Rule 1.5(e) requires only that the client agree in writing to any fee division and that 'the total fee is reasonable', and Georgia RPC 1.5(c)(2) requires a closing statement showing any division. 'That fight is between the two lawyers, not the client' overstates: a quantum meruit claim is legally a claim against the client's recovery (in Ellerin the fee was awarded out of the Brawleys' settlement), and in South Carolina the first lawyer's fee claim runs against the client unless the agreement or the new lawyer assumes it. Fee disputes can go to a court, to arbitration if the agreement provides (Georgia RPC 1.5(b) sets formal requirements for such clauses), or in South Carolina to the Bar's Resolution of Fee Disputes Board (referenced in Tillman). South Carolina: no charging lien for the fee exists at common law — 'the lien protects only costs and disbursements; it does not cover an attorney's fee' — unless the fee agreement creates one (Eleazer).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14(b); Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley (Ga. Ct. App. 2003); Georgia RPC 1.5(b), (c)(2), (e); South Carolina RPC 1.5(e); Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co. (S.C. Ct. App. 1984); Matter of Tillman (S.C. 1995)
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite: 'Here is how it usually works: the first attorney asserts a claim for the reasonable value of the work done (in Georgia, secured by a lien on the case under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14). When the case resolves, that claim is paid out of the attorney-fee share, and the new attorney should confirm in writing that your total fee will not exceed the percentage you originally agreed to — both states require your written agreement to any division of the fee and a total fee that is reasonable (Rule 1.5(e)). If the lawyers cannot agree on the split, the dispute goes to court, to arbitration if your agreement provides for it, or in South Carolina to the Bar's fee-dispute program — and a good successor attorney handles that for you.'

verifiedClaims.claim: This arrangement applies in both workers' compensation claims and standard personal injury lawsuits. The specific lien rules differ between Georgia and South Carolina, as explained below.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Workers' compensation fees are not free-form: in South Carolina 'Attorney fees ... for services under this title are subject to the approval of the commission' and no one may receive a fee for such services 'unless the fee ... is approved by the commission or a court of competent jurisdiction' (S.C. Code § 42-15-90(A), (B)(1)). Say that in workers' compensation cases any fee, including a former attorney's share, must be approved by the workers' compensation agency.
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia's parallel provision (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-108, State Board of Workers' Compensation approval) was not retrievable on Justia today (the year-less URL returned a listing page for every article segment tried) and is not cited in the post; keep the Georgia side general ('the state workers' compensation agency must approve fees') or cite only the South Carolina section. Keep the internal link.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia Rule 1.16(a)(3), an attorney must withdraw if fired by the client. Under Rule 1.16(d), the attorney must return all papers and property the client is entitled to and refund any advance payment of fees not yet earned. A Georgia attorney who refuses to release your file can face disciplinary action from the State Bar of Georgia.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(a)(3), (d) ('surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled and refunding any advance payment of fee that has not been earned'; 'The maximum penalty for a violation of this rule is a public reprimand'); FAO 87-5
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim match on (a)(3) and (d). Optional precision: discipline is imposed by the Supreme Court of Georgia through the State Bar's disciplinary process, and the maximum penalty for a Rule 1.16 violation is a public reprimand.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14, Georgia grants attorneys a charging lien on claims and money due to their clients. This lien attaches to the proceeds of the case, meaning the first attorney's claim follows the money. When the case settles, the new attorney deducts the first attorney's lien from the fee portion before distributing funds.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The statute gives two liens: (a) a retaining lien 'on all papers and money of their clients in their possession for services rendered to them', and (b) 'Upon actions, judgments, and decrees for money, attorneys at law shall have a lien superior to all liens except tax liens; and no person shall be at liberty to satisfy such an action, judgment, or decree until the lien or claim of the attorney for his fees is fully satisfied.' Georgia courts hold the lien 'attaches to fruits of labor and skill of the attorney, whether realized by judgment or decree, or by virtue of an award, or in any other way' (Wooten v. Denmark, 85 Ga. 578 (1890), annotation) and that a § 15-19-14(b) lien 'was fixed as soon as the suit was filed' and 'could not be divested by any subsequent settlement or contract' (Howe & Assocs. v. Daniels, 274 Ga. App. 312 (2005), aff'd 280 Ga. 803 (2006)). So 'attaches to the proceeds of the case' is a fair description of subsection (b); 'on claims and money due to their clients' is loose. The statute secures the fee but 'does not specify how the amount of the fee is to be determined' — that is quantum meruit (Ellerin, quoting Yetman). The last sentence (deducted from the fee portion) is practice, not statute.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14(a)-(b) (2025 Code of Georgia, via Justia) and Justia annotations (Wooten v. Denmark; Howe & Assocs., P.C. v. Daniels; Yetman v. Greer, Klosik & Daugherty; Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley)
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite: 'Under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14, a Georgia attorney has a lien on the client's papers and money in the attorney's possession for services rendered, and a lien on the lawsuit and any judgment or recovery that is superior to every lien except tax liens. Georgia courts treat the lien as attaching to whatever the attorney's work produces — a judgment, an award or a settlement — so the first attorney's claim follows the money. The statute secures the fee but does not set its amount; that is decided in quantum meruit.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia uses the quantum meruit standard to calculate what a terminated attorney is owed. The court considers time spent, complexity of the work, results achieved before termination, and the customary fee for similar services. The terminated attorney does not automatically get their full contingency percentage.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 263 Ga. App. 860, 589 S.E.2d 626 (2003) ('When a contingent fee arrangement exists between a client and an attorney and the client prevents the contingency from happening, the attorney is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees for his services ... the attorney still has [a] remedy in quantum meruit'; 'value is defined in terms of value to the recipient'); Georgia RPC 1.5(a)(1)-(8) (time and labor, novelty and difficulty, customary fee, amount involved and results obtained); Tolson v. Sistrunk, 332 Ga. App. 324 (2015) (origination of the case confers no value on the client)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. Add the Ellerin citation in the body; the point that the discharged lawyer cannot recover the contract percentage because the contingency had not occurred is the holding.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, the statute of limitations for personal injury in Georgia is two years from the date of injury. Georgia also applies a modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, which bars recovery if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more at fault.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33; O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g) ('the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible for the injury or damages claimed')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1756 / facts-1653 (verified 2026-09-24); matches the profile table.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina Rule 1.16 mirrors Georgia's rule. Your attorney must withdraw when you terminate the relationship, must return your file, and must protect your interests during the transition. South Carolina's rule is enforced by the Office of Disciplinary Counsel.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: South Carolina RPC 1.16(a)(3), (d), Rule 407 SCACR; South Carolina Judicial Branch, Lawyer & Judicial Discipline (Office of Disciplinary Counsel / Commission on Lawyer Conduct under the Supreme Court)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. Optional: 'must return your file' → 'must surrender the papers and property you are entitled to' (rule wording; the lawyer may keep copies).

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina recognizes both retaining liens (on documents in the attorney's possession) and charging liens (on the proceeds of litigation).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Half right. South Carolina has no attorney's-lien statute, and its common-law charging lien does not reach the fee: 'While South Carolina recognizes an attorney's lien created by the common law, the lien protects only costs and disbursements; it does not cover an attorney's fee.' A lien for the fee on a judgment or settlement exists only where 'created by an express agreement between an attorney and his client' — an equitable lien by contract (Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., 281 S.C. 344, 315 S.E.2d 174 (Ct. App. 1984)). The common-law retaining lien on the file is recognized (In re Anonymous Member of the S.C. Bar, 287 S.C. 250, 335 S.E.2d 803 (1985); Tillman; White) but sharply limited.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., Inc., 281 S.C. 344, 315 S.E.2d 174 (S.C. Ct. App. 1984); Matter of Tillman, 319 S.C. 461, 462 S.E.2d 283 (1995); In the Matter of White, 328 S.C. 88, 492 S.E.2d 82 (1997)
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite: 'South Carolina has no attorney's-lien statute. Its courts recognize a common-law retaining lien on papers in the attorney's possession, and a common-law lien on a judgment for costs and disbursements only — not for the fee. A lien for the fee on your settlement or judgment exists only if your fee agreement creates one (Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., S.C. Ct. App. 1984), which is why the termination clause in a South Carolina contingency agreement matters.' Same correction in the comparison table's 'Attorney lien statute' row.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina courts have held that a retaining lien cannot be used to hold a client's file hostage when doing so would prejudice the client's case.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: In re Anonymous Member of the S.C. Bar, 287 S.C. 250 (1985) (assertion of a retaining lien 'is not a per se ethical violation' but the attorney must weigh 'whether imposition of the retaining lien would prejudice important rights or interests of the client'); Matter of Tillman, 319 S.C. 461 (1995) (attorney bears the burden of showing 'the client is financially able but deliberately refuses to pay a fee that he has clearly agreed upon and is due'; public reprimand); In the Matter of White, 328 S.C. 88 (1997) (public reprimand for retaining a file as 'a general assurance that whatever interest he may have would be protected')
verifiedClaims.note: Correct and well supported; optionally cite Tillman by name.

verifiedClaims.claim: S.C. Code § 37-5-108 addresses attorney fee reasonableness, and South Carolina courts apply similar standards when evaluating quantum meruit claims by terminated personal injury attorneys. The court examines the amount of work performed, difficulty of the issues, stage of the case at termination, and the eventual result.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 37-5-108 is titled 'Unconscionability; inducement by unconscionable conduct' and sits in the Consumer Protection Code (Title 37, Chapter 5); it governs consumer credit transactions and debt collection and says nothing about attorney fees. The fee-reasonableness standard in South Carolina is Rule 1.5(a), Rule 407 SCACR (time and labor, novelty and difficulty, customary fee, 'the amount involved and the results obtained', whether the fee is fixed or contingent). For a discharged lawyer: 'An attorney is entitled to the reasonable value of the services performed for his client in the absence of a controlling contract' (Eleazer), the discharge is 'subject to liability for payment for the lawyer's services' (Rule 1.16 cmt [4]), and the SC Bar's Ethics Advisory Committee notes a discharged contingent-fee lawyer 'may ... be able to recover in quantum meruit for the reasonable value of the services' but may not bill hourly unless the agreement so provides (EAO 02-08).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 37-5-108 (scstatehouse.gov); South Carolina RPC 1.5(a), Rule 407 SCACR; Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co. (S.C. Ct. App. 1984); South Carolina RPC 1.16 comment [4]; SC Bar Ethics Advisory Opinion 02-08
verifiedClaims.note: Drop the § 37-5-108 citation everywhere it appears (body, key takeaways, faq:1). Replacement paragraph: 'South Carolina measures every fee, including a discharged lawyer's, against the reasonableness factors in Rule 1.5(a) of the Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 407, SCACR): the time and labor required, the difficulty of the issues, the fee customarily charged, and the amount involved and results obtained. verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's 2-year (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) statutes of limitations make prompt action critical.

Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to terminate your attorney at any time and for any reason. This right is protected under each state's Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.16). Your lawyer cannot hold your case hostage, and they must return your file and cooperate with the transition to your new attorney.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(a)(3), (d); South Carolina RPC 1.16(a)(3), (d) and cmt [4]; Tillman (S.C. 1995)
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data; accurate as written.

verifiedClaims.claim: Possibly. If your first lawyer worked on a contingency fee basis, they may be entitled to a portion of the fee based on work already completed. In Georgia, attorneys can assert a lien under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14. In South Carolina, fee disputes are governed by the reasonableness standard under S.C. Code § 37-5-108 and the Rules of Professional Conduct. Your new attorney can help negotiate or dispute any unreasonable lien.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Possibly. A lawyer you discharge before your case resolves cannot collect the contract percentage, but may claim the reasonable value of the work already done. In Georgia that claim is secured by a lien on the case under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14 and measured in quantum meruit (Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 2003). South Carolina has no attorney's-lien statute; the claim is measured by the reasonableness factors in Rule 1.5(a) of the Rules of Professional Conduct, and a lien on your recovery exists only if your fee agreement creates one (Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., 1984). Your new attorney can negotiate or dispute any unreasonable claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14; Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 263 Ga. App. 860 (2003); Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., 281 S.C. 344 (Ct. App. 1984); South Carolina RPC 1.5(a); S.C. Code § 37-5-108 (unrelated)
verifiedClaims.note: The § 37-5-108 citation is wrong (Consumer Protection Code unconscionability) and this answer is republished as FAQPage structured data, so the error is published twice. Remove it.

verifiedClaims.claim: While you always have the right to fire your attorney, switching becomes more difficult once a case is close to trial. A judge may deny a continuance request if changing lawyers would significantly delay proceedings. Switching is easiest during the investigation, treatment, or pre-litigation negotiation phases.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: USCR 4.3(1) (withdrawal may be denied where it 'would delay the trial'); South Carolina RPC 1.16(c); Rule 11(b), SCRCP

verifiedClaims.claim: Common red flags include unreturned phone calls or emails for weeks at a time, no case updates, pressure to accept a low settlement, lack of experience with your case type, your case being handed off to junior associates without notice, and missed deadlines or filing errors. Trust your instincts — if you feel your case is not being prioritized, it may be time for a change.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.4(a) and South Carolina RPC 1.4(a) (duty to keep the client reasonably informed and promptly comply with reasonable requests for information); advice otherwise
verifiedClaims.note: No figure asserted; 'for weeks at a time' is safely within Rule 1.4.

verifiedClaims.claim: First, consult with a new attorney to confirm they will take your case. Then send written notice to your current attorney terminating the relationship. Request your complete case file in writing. Your former attorney must comply and transfer your file. Your new lawyer will handle the transition, review the file, and continue your case from where it left off.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia RPC 1.16(a)(3), (d); South Carolina RPC 1.16(a)(3), (d); FAO 87-5
verifiedClaims.note: Optional: add 'If a lawsuit is already pending, the change of counsel also goes through the court (Uniform Superior Court Rule 4.3 in Georgia; Rule 11(b), SCRCP in South Carolina).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Not if done properly and promptly. A better attorney who is responsive, experienced, and aggressive will almost always improve your outcome compared to staying with one who is neglecting your case. The key is to switch early enough that your new lawyer has time to build the strongest possible case before any deadlines or trial dates.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Not if done properly and promptly. A responsive, experienced attorney can improve your outcome compared with staying with one who is neglecting your case. The key is to switch early enough that your new lawyer has time to build the strongest possible case before any deadlines or trial dates.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: No study supports 'almost always'; softened rather than sourced
